text:
Post-9/11 GI Bill: the basics

The Post-9/11 GI Bill provides up to 36 months of education benefits. You generally qualify with at least 90 days of aggregate active-duty service after September 10, 2001, or if you were discharged with a service-connected disability after 30 days. Your benefit level is 40% to 100% depending on how long you served.

When you use it at an approved school, the benefit can pay tuition and fees directly to the school, a monthly housing allowance based on the school's ZIP code, and a yearly books and supplies stipend. Benefit levels and rates are set by VA; confirm your own percentage by applying for a Certificate of Eligibility.
title: Post-9/11 GI Bill: the basics

text:
Forever GI Bill: time limits on using your benefit

If your last discharge or release from active duty was on or after January 1, 2013, your Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits do not expire. There is no 15-year time limit for you.

If your last discharge or release was before January 1, 2013, your benefits generally expire 15 years after your last period of active duty of at least 90 consecutive days. Some exceptions apply, so veterans in this group should confirm their own end date with VA before making plans.
title: Forever GI Bill: time limits on using your benefit

text:
Transferring GI Bill benefits to family members

Eligible service members can transfer unused Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits to a spouse or children. To be eligible you must be on active duty or in the Selected Reserve, have at least 6 years of service, and agree to serve 4 more years.

The transfer must be requested while you are still serving, through the Department of Defense (milConnect). You cannot request a transfer after you have separated or retired. Once transferred, the family member applies to VA for the benefit.
title: Transferring GI Bill benefits to family members

text:
VA disability compensation: how it works

VA disability compensation is a monthly, tax-free payment for veterans with conditions connected to their military service. VA assigns a disability rating from 0% to 100% in 10% steps; the rating is based on the evidence in your claim.

Payment rates change every year on December 1 with the cost-of-living adjustment. Always check the current-year rate table on VA.gov for the amount that matches your rating and dependents. The effective date of your benefit is usually the date VA receives your claim. Filing an Intent to File (VA Form 21-0966) can protect that date for up to one year while you gather evidence.
title: VA disability compensation: how it works

text:
How to file a VA claim and check your claim status

You can file a VA disability claim online at VA.gov, by mail, in person at a regional office, or with help from an accredited representative. To use VA.gov you sign in with a Login.gov or ID.me account.

To check the status of a claim or appeal, sign in to VA.gov and open your claim status page. You can also upload evidence there. If you do not have an account yet, create one first; the older eBenefits and DS Logon sign-in options are being retired for these tasks.
title: How to file a VA claim and check your claim status

text:
VA health care: who can enroll

Most veterans who served in the active military and were discharged under conditions other than dishonorable can apply for VA health care. VA places enrolled veterans into priority groups 1 through 8, which affect copays and wait for some services.

You can apply online at VA.gov, by phone, by mail, or in person at a VA medical center. Veterans who served in locations with certain toxic exposures may qualify for enrollment under expanded eligibility rules (see the PACT Act overview). Having a VA disability rating can place you in a higher priority group.
title: VA health care: who can enroll

text:
PACT Act: toxic exposures and presumptive conditions

The PACT Act, signed in August 2022, expanded VA health care and disability benefits for veterans exposed to burn pits, Agent Orange and other toxins. It added many presumptive conditions: if you served in a covered location during a covered period and have a listed condition, VA presumes the condition is service connected.

Veterans who served in Iraq, Afghanistan and other listed Southwest Asia locations may have been exposed to burn pits. You can use the VA.gov screening tools to see whether you may be eligible, and you can apply for health care or file a claim at any time. VA makes the final eligibility decision.
title: PACT Act: toxic exposures and presumptive conditions

text:
VA home loan benefit: basics

The VA home loan guaranty helps eligible veterans, service members and some surviving spouses buy, build or refinance a home. Most VA-backed loans do not require a down payment and do not require private mortgage insurance.

You start by requesting a Certificate of Eligibility (COE). Most borrowers pay a one-time VA funding fee, but veterans who receive VA disability compensation are exempt from the funding fee. VA does not make the loan itself: private lenders set interest rates and credit requirements, so compare offers from more than one lender.
title: VA home loan benefit: basics

text:
Veterans Crisis Line

If you are a veteran in crisis or you are worried about one, support is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, free and confidential. Dial 988 and then press 1. You can also text 838255 or chat online at VeteransCrisisLine.net. Family members and friends can use these services too.

If someone is in immediate danger, call 911.
title: Veterans Crisis Line

text:
Transition Assistance Program (TAP)

TAP is a required program for separating service members. It includes workshops on benefits, career planning and resume writing. Service members should begin transition planning as early as possible: at least 12 months before separation, or 24 months before retirement.

Your installation's transition office schedules TAP. Completing TAP is also how you build an Individual Transition Plan, which is a prerequisite for programs such as SkillBridge.
title: Transition Assistance Program (TAP)

text:
DoD SkillBridge

SkillBridge lets eligible service members gain civilian work experience through an internship or training with an industry partner during their last 180 days of service. Participants continue to receive their military pay and benefits.

You need your commander's approval and must have completed required transition steps first. Program availability varies by service branch and installation, so start the conversation with your transition office well before the 180-day window opens.
title: DoD SkillBridge

text:
Translating your MOS into a civilian resume

Recruiters do not speak military. Replace jargon with plain language, quantify results (people led, equipment value, budget managed), and map your duties to the skills in the job post. Use a skills-based format and keep it to one or two pages.

Military.com's MOS-to-civilian tool suggests common civilian job titles; treat them as starting points and tailor each resume to the specific listing.
title: Translating your MOS into a civilian resume

text:
Using the Military.com job board

Search the job board by keyword, location or military occupation code, filter by security clearance, and save searches to get email alerts. Employers listed as veteran-friendly have confirmed their hiring programs with us.

Create a profile and upload a resume to apply faster. We never charge job seekers to apply.
title: Using the Military.com job board

text:
Military discounts: how verification works

Many retailers and restaurants offer military and veteran discounts, but programs, amounts and eligibility vary by company and by store, and they can change without notice. Most online retailers verify status through a third-party service such as ID.me or SheerID; in stores you may be asked for a military ID, VA ID card or discharge papers.

Always confirm the offer with the retailer before you buy. Discounts are never guaranteed.
title: Military discounts: how verification works

text:
State veterans benefits: overview

Many states offer their own veterans benefits, such as property tax exemptions, tuition assistance, special license plates and hiring preferences. Eligibility and amounts differ widely from state to state and are set by each state.

For details, contact your state's Department of Veterans Affairs or county veterans service office. This article does not list state-by-state rules.
title: State veterans benefits: overview

text:
Accredited representatives and VSOs: free help with claims

Veterans Service Organizations (VSOs), state and county veteran service officers, and other VA-accredited representatives can help you file and manage claims at no cost. You can search for an accredited representative on VA.gov.

It is against the law for anyone to charge you a fee for help preparing or filing an initial claim. Be careful of companies that promise higher ratings in exchange for money.
title: Accredited representatives and VSOs: free help with claims

text:
What the GI Bill can pay for

Depending on the benefit you are eligible for, GI Bill education benefits can be used for undergraduate and graduate degrees, vocational and technical training, non-college degree programs, apprenticeships and on-the-job training, licensing and certification tests, and flight training.

The school or program must be approved for VA benefits. Use the VA GI Bill Comparison Tool to check whether a specific school or program is approved and what you can expect to receive.
title: What the GI Bill can pay for

text:
How the Military.com assistant uses your data

The assistant only uses information from your profile (such as branch, service dates, disability rating, state and dependents) to personalize answers if you have turned on personalization. If personalization is off, the assistant answers using only what you type in the chat.

Do not enter Social Security numbers, VA file numbers, bank details or medical records in the chat. The assistant cannot access your VA account or look up claims. Chat logs are kept for 30 days and are scrubbed of personal identifiers before storage.
title: How the Military.com assistant uses your data

text:
Dependents' Educational Assistance (DEA)

DEA provides education and training benefits to eligible children and spouses of veterans who died or are permanently and totally disabled because of a service-connected condition. Eligible family members may receive up to 36 months of benefits.

DEA is separate from Post-9/11 GI Bill transfer. Eligibility is determined by VA based on the veteran's service-connected disability status; apply through VA.gov.
title: Dependents' Educational Assistance (DEA)
